summary: This Best Current Practice sets a policy for moderating disruptive participation across the IETF's public mailing lists and other discussion channels. It sets guardrails for moderation and creates a moderator team that will develop procedures and apply them consistently alongside chairs and administrators. It obsoletes RFC 3683 and RFC 3934 and updates RFC 2418 and RFC 9245.

plainLanguage.summary: The IETF does its work in public mailing lists, chat rooms and shared tools, and from time to time somebody disrupts one of them. This document sets out who handles that and what they may do. It creates a team of moderators, says that working group chairs and list owners handle most cases themselves, and gives a chain of appeals when someone disagrees with a decision. The aim is to keep the forum open and civil, not to punish anyone.

subtitle: How the IETF handles people who disrupt its mailing lists, chats and other public forums.

tldr.problem: The IETF discusses its work in public mailing lists, chats and collaborative tools, and any open forum eventually sees behaviour that disrupts it. Earlier processes for handling that were inconsistent and left the same actions spelled differently in several documents.
tldr.mechanism: The document creates a moderator team appointed by the IESG, sets out what participants, administrators, moderators and area directors each do, and lists the actions that may be taken and how they must be reported.
tldr.outcome: This document replaced RFC 3683 and RFC 3934 and updates RFC 2418 and RFC 9245. It is a Best Current Practice, and its procedures take effect only once the IESG approves them.

today: RFC 9945 is a Best Current Practice document. It replaced RFC 3683 and RFC 3934, and updates RFC 2418 and RFC 9245. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Policy Covers
sections.content:
This memo establishes a policy for the moderation of disruptive participation across the IETF's various public online contribution channels and discussion fora. It creates a moderator team to develop the procedures and to facilitate their consistent application.

The memo replaces earlier processes. It obsoletes RFC 3683, whose posting rights action is replaced by the processes defined here, and obsoletes RFC 3934, which set out working group moderation procedures. It obsoletes Section 3 of RFC 9245 and the second paragraph of Section 4 of RFC 9245, because the moderator team defined here replaces the IETF discussion list moderator team. It updates Section 6.1 of RFC 2418, because the moderator team will work together with working group chairs to moderate disruptive behaviour.

The processes apply only to IETF activities, and not to related organisations such as the Internet Research Task Force, the Internet Architecture Board, the RFC Series Working Group, the RFC Series Approval Board or the Independent RFC Submission Stream, without their explicit agreement. The changes take effect when the procedures described in Section 4 have been approved by the IESG.

The memo uses the term administrator for the people the IESG assigns to manage a public participation channel or forum, and forum for any public IETF participation channel, such as a mailing list, a chat group, or a discussion in a collaborative tool such as GitHub or GitLab. Working group chairs are administrators of the public fora their groups use, and the owners of non-working-group IETF mailing lists are another example of administrators.
sections.plainLanguage: This document covers every public place the IETF talks: mailing lists, chat groups and shared tools. It replaces three older sets of rules and changes one section of the working group charter rules.

sections.title: The Goals of Moderation
sections.content:
The cornerstone of the policy is that individuals are responsible for furthering the goals of the IETF as an organisation in a manner consistent with the IETF community's own code of conduct.

Disagreement and diverse points of view within any standards organisation are to be expected and are even healthy. The IETF is an open standards organisation with a discussion-based rough consensus process, so engaged, respectful discussion that is within the scope of an IETF forum should not be considered disruptive, and someone should not be considered disruptive solely because they are outside the rough consensus. However, when someone crosses the line into disruptive behaviour, action must be taken in order to maintain the decorum of the community.

The moderation policy goals are to apply consistent, fair and timely moderation across all public online IETF participation channels and fora, without regard to a participant's role in the IETF or previous technical contributions; to ensure that appeals are available to address disagreements about moderation actions; to balance transparency against both the privacy of individuals involved and further disruption to the community; to allow moderation decisions to be reconsidered; and to provide the broadest possible latitude to all people doing moderation, so that they have the flexibility to address a broad range of individuals and circumstances.

The objective is explicitly not punishment, but to maintain an open, welcoming, non-hostile environment in which all may participate on an equal footing, regardless of their role in the IETF or past technical contributions.
sections.plainLanguage: Disagreement is expected and healthy in an open standards process. Moderation is for behaviour that breaks the forum, not for opinions that lose. The goal is a welcoming place where everyone is on equal footing, and the document says outright that this is not about punishment.

sections.title: The Moderator Team
sections.content:
A moderator team for the IETF develops and maintains guidelines for moderation and facilitates their consistent implementation and application.

The IESG appoints and recalls moderators. The moderator team initially consists of no fewer than five individuals, and it may expand or contract based on operational experience. In selecting members, the IESG takes into account geographic coverage, expected and unexpected absences, and team diversity.

Because the IESG and the IAB are in the appeals chain for moderator team decisions, the IESG must not appoint a moderator who is serving on the IESG or the IAB. Individuals serving on other bodies to which NomCom appoints members, such as the IETF Trust or the IETF LLC Board, as well as IETF LLC staff and contractors, are also excluded from serving on the moderator team. If a moderator assumes any such role, they step down from the moderator team soon after.

Due to the global nature of the IETF, the membership of the team should reflect a diversity of time zones and other participant characteristics that lets it operate effectively around the clock and throughout the year. Ideally the moderators should be able to respond to issues within a few hours. Team diversity also improves the likelihood that any participant experiencing or observing disruptive behaviour can identify a moderator they feel comfortable contacting.

The IETF is committed to providing and funding training for administrators and moderators as necessary, and the IESG negotiates any required funding or resources with IETF Administration LLC.
sections.plainLanguage: The IESG appoints a team of at least five moderators. They must not also sit on the IESG or the IAB, because those bodies hear appeals against their decisions. The team should cover the world's time zones so it can answer quickly at any hour.

sections.title: Who Does What
sections.content:
The policy applies to all public online IETF fora, both present and future, including but not limited to mailing lists, chat groups, and discussions in other systems the IETF or its working groups have chosen to employ, such as GitHub repositories, wikis or issue trackers.

Participants should always behave in the manner described in the philosophy section. They are also encouraged to report disruptive behaviour directed at them or at someone else to an administrator of the forum and to the moderators.

Administrators are primarily responsible for managing their fora in accordance with procedures developed by the moderators and approved by the IESG. They must address reports of disruptive behaviour in a timely fashion, telling the moderators about reports or actions taken. They may amend or rescind actions, including those taken by the moderator team, after consulting with that team. For a working group, the chairs are by default the administrators. They may delegate this responsibility, but they must always accept, acknowledge and keep track of complaints of disruptive behaviour. Forum administrators should perform moderation in a way that obviates the need for moderator team involvement.

Moderators are responsible for establishing procedures that address moderation needs across all IETF fora, present and future, and are a resource the community can use to address disruptive behaviour. The team is responsible to the IESG, which will create or designate a forum to facilitate discussion about moderation and refer interested parties to it. Moderators may take actions when administrators do not respond to reports in a timely fashion, and their first action should generally be to attempt to contact and advise the relevant administrators. They should only take moderation actions when administrators are not responsive, or when someone disrupts multiple fora at the same time. Moderators should generally give working group chairs the opportunity to manage what may be difficult and contentious debates within their groups. Moderators must notify administrators of any actions they take. They are administrators for IETF plenary fora, currently the IETF discussion and Last Call lists and any plenary chat sessions, and for any forum that does not otherwise have an administrator. To scale the function, except for plenary fora, moderators are not expected to always actively monitor all communications; in general they process reports from participants.

Area directors are expected to resolve conflicts, and the IESG will periodically evaluate the performance and needs of moderators and may appoint and recall them as it deems appropriate. Apart from that, the IESG refrains from the day-to-day operation and management of the moderator team, though the moderators may consult with the IESG when needed.

Unsolicited bulk messages are considered disruptive and should be handled in a manner consistent with the IESG statement on spam control on IETF mailing lists or its successors. Administrators and moderators may take similar actions in other fora, and such actions require no additional reporting.
sections.plainLanguage: Most problems are handled by the person who already runs the list, usually a working group chair, and the moderators only step in when that person will not act or when the same person is disrupting several fora at once. The moderators are also the administrators for the plenary lists and for any forum nobody else looks after.

sections.title: Moderation Actions and Reporting
sections.content:
Within the bounds of the policy, the moderator team develops and maintains the procedures and criteria for moderation, including the moderator team's own operating procedures. Those procedures and criteria are developed with community input, approved by the IESG before going into effect, and made public. They need not be documented in the RFC Series. This is the team's first task, and until those procedures and criteria are established, all the previous processes referenced in the introduction remain in effect.

The intent of the memo is to give the widest possible freedom of action to administrators and moderators, with the expectation that the minimal actions necessary will be taken. Those directed to stop disrupting a forum must do so immediately, and further disruptions may lead to further corrective actions.

Examples of actions that could be taken include automated rate-limiting mechanisms; review and approval of submissions and messages; a private or public admonishment; and temporary or indefinite suspension of participation privileges in one or more fora. These are only examples and are not in any way prescriptive. Administrators and moderators are free to decide on these or other actions.

All moderation actions that restrict participation privileges must be immediately reported to those they take effect against, to relevant administrators, and to the moderator team for their review. They must also be reported periodically to the IESG.

Only moderation actions suspending participation privileges for longer than fourteen days must be reported to the forum to which the action applies, or at any event at the request of the suspended person. If such an action applies to more than one forum, it should be communicated to the community in a manner decided by the IESG. The moderators will periodically provide an aggregate report to the community on actions taken under this policy.

Moderator actions are only permitted for the purpose of limiting disruptive communications in online IETF fora. All other actions are out of scope. Examples of out-of-scope actions include Datatracker account removal, restriction of in-person, virtual or hybrid meeting participation, content removal or redaction, and moderation or policing of private or non-IETF communications. While the moderator team does not moderate non-public IETF mailing lists, the administrators of such lists can choose to adopt some of the procedures the team develops.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of possible actions is short and left to the administrator's judgement: rate limiting, reviewing messages before they go out, a private or public telling-off, and suspending someone's participation for a while or for good. Anyone suspended must be told straight away, and the wider community only hears about it when the suspension runs past fourteen days.

sections.title: Conflict Resolution and Reinstatement
sections.content:
Administrators and moderators must act in a manner consistent with this memo and with the guidelines approved by the IESG. In cases of disagreement over a moderation decision, anyone may take the matter up with the responsible area director for resolution, or with the IETF Chair if a responsible area director cannot be determined or is not assigned. If the disagreement cannot be resolved by the area director, that person may then appeal to the IESG and subsequently to the IAB using the processes stated in Sections 6.5.1 and 6.5.4 of RFC 2026.

People and circumstances change. Individuals whose participation privileges have been indefinitely suspended from a forum may request reinstatement. Requests for reinstatement may be made no earlier than a year after the initial decision, and then only annually afterwards.

Any such request must be directed to the entity that made the decision, for example the moderator team or the working group chairs, or their successors. That party may at its discretion reinstate someone, conditionally or unconditionally. To avoid denial-of-service attacks on IETF processes, decisions not to reinstate someone's participation privileges cannot be appealed. Any reinstatement is a grace and not a right.

A suspension of participation privileges imposed before this process existed is reconsidered only in accordance with the processes in place at the time of the suspension, even if the corresponding RFC has since been formally obsoleted.
sections.plainLanguage: If you think a moderation decision was wrong, you can take it to the area director, then to the IESG, then to the IAB. Someone suspended for good can ask to be let back in, but not for a year, and then only once a year. Being let back in is a favour, not an entitlement, and a refusal cannot be appealed.

sections.title: Relationship to Other IETF Functions
sections.content:
Administrators and moderators must complement the efforts of the IETF Ombudsteam, whose focus on anti-harassment remains unchanged. Administrators and moderators should always report suspected harassment. They should nonetheless take any necessary actions regarding disruptive behaviour.

The Board of Directors of IETF Administration LLC has a fiduciary duty for the overall organisation, which includes the duty to protect the organisation from serious legal risk that may arise from the behaviour of IETF participants. This protection may include the need for the LLC to take emergency moderation actions. These emergency actions are expected to be taken only when the LLC has received legal advice that such an action is necessary, and so are expected to be extremely rare in frequency. Examples of where this might be necessary are someone making a credible threat of harm to other IETF participants; someone using IETF mailing lists and websites to share content where publishing it on those lists or sites brings serious legal risk to the IETF; and someone making a credible threat of legal action where any form of interaction with them on IETF mailing lists may have serious legal consequences for the IETF.

If any such action is taken, the IETF LLC should, except where limited by legal advice to the contrary, inform the IESG as soon as possible, providing full details of the subject of the action, the nature of the action, the reason and the expected duration. The LLC should also inform the moderator team and the IETF community, except where it receives legal advice to the contrary.

Because such an action is taken by the IETF LLC in order to protect the IETF according to its fiduciary duty, it cannot be overridden by a decision of the moderator team or the IESG. The subject of the action may request a review by the IETF LLC Board. Any such action taken under this part of the policy is not subject to the rest of the policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Harassment complaints go to the Ombudsteam, and the two efforts sit side by side rather than one replacing the other. Separately, the organisation's legal body can act in an emergency when there is a serious legal risk, and that action cannot be overturned by the moderator team.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document states that the usual security considerations do not apply to it. Nothing else is said about security in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: This document says the usual security boilerplate does not apply, and says nothing further about security.

viz.caption: THE FIVE GOALS OF THE MODERATION POLICY

items.title: Consistent and fair
items.text: Apply the same moderation across all IETF fora, whatever a participant's role or track record.

items.title: Appeals available
items.text: Make sure there is a way to challenge a moderation action.

items.title: Balance
items.text: Balance transparency against the privacy of the people involved and against more disruption.

items.title: Reconsideration
items.text: Allow moderation decisions to be reconsidered.

items.title: Wide latitude
items.text: Give those doing the moderating room to handle many kinds of person and situation.

viz.caption: THE FOUR ROLES AND WHAT EACH DOES

cells: Behave well, and report disruptive behaviour to an administrator and to the moderators
Run their own fora, act on reports promptly, and tell the moderators what they did
Set the procedures, and act only when administrators will not or when several fora are hit at once

messages.label: ESCALATE WHEN THE ADMINISTRATOR DOES NOT RESPOND
APPEAL TO THE IESG
messages.note: And afterwards to the IAB, using the processes in RFC 2026.
